classification.difficultyReason: Use folding invariants to derive a smaller triangle's symbolic integer side lengths, then connect its preserved shape and smaller size to the supplied minimality assumption to obtain a contradiction.

inlines.text: Consider the right-angled isosceles triangle shown below. We will prove that its side lengths cannot be integers.
We will start the proof by assuming that this is the
right-angled isosceles triangle with integer sides.

spec.description: Unlabelled right-angled isosceles triangle with horizontal and vertical legs m and rising hypotenuse n.
spec.mathematics: Two perpendicular equal legs of length m; hypotenuse n.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied side labels and right-angle marker are visible.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If the triangle were made from paper, then we could fold $B$ onto $AC$ at $E$. The fold bisects $\angle A$ (divides it into two equal angles) and intersects the opposite side at $D$. Find the angles in $\triangle DEC$.

spec.description: ABC with E on AC, D on BC, dashed fold AD and dashed segment ED. Decorative pale cyan fill omitted.
spec.mathematics: AB = BC; angle ABC is right; AD bisects angle BAC; reflection across AD sends B to E.
spec.answerVisibility: No derived angles or side lengths supplied.

answer.short:
$\angle DEC=90^\circ$, $\angle ECD=45^\circ$, $\angle EDC=45^\circ$.

Folding preserves the right angle at $B$; the remaining angles follow from the original isosceles triangle and its angle sum.
answer.worked:
Since $AB=BC$ and $\angle ABC=90^\circ$, the equal base angles are
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAC&=\frac{180^\circ-90^\circ}{2}\\\angle BAC&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\angle ECD=\angle ACB=45^\circ$. Folding sends $AB$ to $AE$ and $DB$ to $DE$, so $\angle AED=90^\circ$. Since $A,E,C$ are collinear, $\angle DEC=90^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle EDC&=180^\circ-90^\circ-45^\circ\\\angle EDC&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, find the side lengths of $\triangle DEC$ in terms of $m$ and $n$.

answer.short:
$EC=ED=n-m$, $DC=2m-n$.

Use lengths preserved by folding and subtract along $AC$ and $BC$.
answer.worked:
Folding preserves lengths, so $AE=AB=m$ and $DE=DB$. From part (a), $\triangle DEC$ is isosceles, so $DE=EC$.
$$\begin{align*}EC&=AC-AE\\EC&=n-m,\\ED&=EC\\ED&=n-m,\\DC&=BC-BD\\DC&=m-(n-m)\\DC&=2m-n.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Conclude that $\triangle DEC$ also has integer side lengths. Why is this impossible?

answer.short: Its sides $n-m$, $n-m$ and $2m-n$ are integers. It is a smaller right-angled isosceles triangle, contradicting the assumed minimality of $\triangle ABC$.
answer.worked: Since $m$ and $n$ are integers, $n-m$ and $2m-n$ are integers. Part (a) shows that $\triangle DEC$ is right-angled and isosceles. Its hypotenuse $DC$ is a proper part of $BC$, so $DC<m<n$; hence it is smaller than $\triangle ABC$. This contradicts the assumption that $\triangle ABC$ is the smallest right-angled isosceles triangle with integer sides. Therefore no such triangle has integer side lengths.
